goal: Clay and pots: at the potter's wheel throw three pots (1-4) and name each one, use the clay lens (C) and look around with it, break a pot (B), then read what opened in the codex (Tab). Then carry on toward dusk as far as your time allows, and answer the questions at the end.

findings.title: Aiming at a pot on the drying board takes several tries
findings.detail: Standing at the board the pots are small and below eye level; the 'B break the <name>' prompt appears only with the crosshair on a pot within reach, and getting there took several look adjustments. Breaking worked once aimed.
findings.repro: throw three pots, C, walk to the drying board, try to aim B at a pot

findings.title: Place label drawn over the HUD's CHORES header
findings.detail: Walking to the wheel, the 'The potter's wheel' label sits on the same line as 'CHORES' and the two overlap.
findings.repro: pt start --seed 2; walk toward the wheel

findings.title: Codex list clips long titles
findings.detail: 'The space in the pot' shows as 'The space in the po' at the edge of the list panel at 640x360. Known.

verdict: The clay chapter reads well: three named pots, the lens re-labels MADE as 'clay' and greys the world, breaking one leaves shards, and the codex pages (Chandogya 6.1.4, Karika 3.3-4, Other schools) explain it with sources. Carried on to dusk and turned one snake to rope. Only HUD/aiming friction. secondsToObjective are wall-clock seconds from pt start (no probe); this session was driven by the proctor, interleaved with another session, on a shared machine, so the times are long. The proctor had read the #39 diff, so this is not a naive first-time read.

answers.question: In your own words, what did you think the game was about? What did the rope and the snake, and the clay and the pots, mean?
answers.answer: The named pots are one clay: the names and shapes are real as uses but the stuff is one, and breaking a pot loses nothing of the clay. The snake on the path was a rope all along; fear came from not seeing in poor light and ended when I held the lamp and looked steadily. Sleep extends it: waking, dream and deep sleep came and went, and the waking text says you were there for all three.

answers.question: Did anything feel preachy, confusing, or inaccurate (in the teaching, the verses in the codex, or how the tradition is described)? Say what and where; if nothing did, say so.
answers.answer: Nothing felt preachy: the game shows, and the codex quotes its sources with Sanskrit and a named translation. 'Other schools' gives Visistadvaita and Dvaita fair, short readings and says the game follows one school. I cannot judge the translations, some of which are marked as working translations awaiting review.
